title: Apply the theories, principles, techniques and tools of group dynamics to extension practice in a simple group setting

lessons.title: Why groups matter in extension
lessons.html:
Working through groups

Much South African extension work happens with groups: farmer study groups, co-operatives, communal grazing committees, women's vegetable gardens, irrigation scheme user associations and Community Property Associations on land reform farms. Groups allow a practitioner to reach more people, pool resources such as a shared tractor or bulk feed order, and give members support and accountability.

Types of groups

  • Formal groups have a constitution, office bearers and registration, such as a registered primary co-operative.
  • Informal groups form around shared interests, such as neighbours who share a borehole.
  • Task groups are created for a specific job, for example a committee to repair the dip tank.

Stages of group development

Bruce Tuckman's model describes five stages:

  1. Forming - members are polite and uncertain; they look to the facilitator for direction.
  2. Storming - conflict arises over roles, money and leadership.
  3. Norming - the group agrees on rules and ways of working.
  4. Performing - the group works effectively towards its goals.
  5. Adjourning - the group ends or changes when the task is completed.

Groups do not always move neatly forward; a new member, a failed harvest or a dispute about money can push a group back into storming. Recognising the stage helps you choose the right support. In forming, provide structure and clear information. In storming, help the group surface and resolve conflict openly. In norming, support the group to write down rules. In performing, step back and let the group lead.

lessons.title: Roles, leadership and communication in groups
lessons.html:
Understanding what happens inside a group

Group dynamics are the forces that shape how members interact: who speaks, who decides, who is ignored and how conflict is handled.

Member roles

TypeExamples
Task rolesInitiator, information giver, summariser, timekeeper
Maintenance rolesEncourager, harmoniser, gatekeeper who invites quiet members to speak
Blocking rolesDominator, blocker, joker who distracts, member who withdraws

A healthy group has a good balance of task and maintenance roles. The facilitator can model these roles and gently manage blocking behaviour.

Leadership styles

  • Autocratic - leader decides alone; quick but may lose commitment.
  • Democratic - decisions through discussion and voting; slower but builds ownership.
  • Laissez-faire - little direction; can work for mature groups but leaves new groups lost.

In rural settings, leadership may also come from traditional authorities, church leaders or older men. Respect these structures while making sure women and youth also have a voice.

Communication patterns

Watch whether all communication flows through one person, or whether members talk to each other. Note who sits at the back and never speaks. Language matters: run meetings in the language the members are most comfortable with, such as isiZulu, Sesotho or Afrikaans, and use interpreters when needed.

Cohesion and groupthink

Cohesion keeps members committed, but very cohesive groups can fall into groupthink, where nobody challenges a bad decision, such as buying an expensive tractor without a business plan. Encourage members to raise concerns and consider alternatives.

lessons.title: Techniques and tools for working with a group
lessons.html:
Practical facilitation tools

Group dynamics theory becomes useful when it guides what you do in a meeting. These techniques suit a simple group setting such as a 15-member vegetable project.

Techniques for participation

  • Ice-breakers to relax members at the start.
  • Brainstorming where all ideas are written down without criticism.
  • Small group work in threes or fours so that quiet members can speak.
  • Round robin where each person speaks in turn.
  • Ranking and scoring with stones or beans on the ground to prioritise problems; this works well with members who cannot read.

Tools for analysing the group

  • Sociogram - a diagram showing who interacts with whom, revealing cliques and isolated members.
  • Venn diagram - circles showing the institutions that matter to the group and how close they are.
  • Observation checklist - notes on roles, participation and decisions during a meeting.

Managing conflict

  1. Acknowledge the conflict calmly; do not ignore it.
  2. Let each side explain its view without interruption.
  3. Focus on interests, such as fair access to water, rather than positions.
  4. Look for options together and agree on a way forward.
  5. Record agreements in the minutes and follow up.

Where conflict involves money, help the group set up transparent record-keeping, such as two signatories on the bank account and a treasurer's report at every meeting.

Key points

  • Groups move through forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning.
  • Balance task and maintenance roles and manage blocking roles.
  • Choose a leadership style that suits the group's maturity.
  • Use participatory techniques such as small groups and ranking with stones.
  • Handle conflict openly, focusing on interests rather than positions.
